newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil says U.S. offer of anti-drug money laughable.
newsitem.headline: Brazil says U.S. offer of anti-drug money laughable.

text.p: Brazil on Tuesday surprised the United States by rejecting a "laughable" $600,000 from Washington to help it fight the drug war.

Government sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Justice Minister Nelson Jobim refused to accept the money because it was a derisory sum compared with the seriousness of the problem and with aid other Latin American countries receive.

"It just isn't enough," said one source, noting that in 1995 Washington gave $50 million and 15 airplanes to Bolivia, $30 million and six helicopters to Colombia and $30 million to Peru. "What's $600,000?"
The U.S. embassy in Brasilia said it had not been advised or warned of Jobim's decision. "U.S.-Brazilian relations have never been better," it said in a statement.

"In this context we were surprised and disappointed to read in the media comments by (Brazilian) officials questioning the utility of a longstanding U.S. programme of cooperation and assistance in combating drug abuse and trafficking," the embassy said.

The $600,000 was offered to Brazil by the State Department's International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs to help combat the drug trade next year. The U.S. embassy said it was part of a longstanding programme to which Washington had contributed about $16 million over the past 22 years.
Jobim's decision was supported by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. Cardoso's spokesman Sergio Amaral said the president "had full confidence" that Jobim had his reasons.
A Justice Ministry spokesman said Jobim was not concerned about the furore his decision had stirred in U.S. diplomatic and anti-narcotics circles.
"He's not worried because he does not think this will affect the otherwise solid cooperation between the two countries on the drugs front," the spokesman said.
The Justice Ministry took pains to stress that Brazil's battle against the narcotics trade did not depend on outside help, which was, nevertheless, always welcome.

Brazil planned to invest next year up to $600 million in anti-drug operations and infrastructure, including tighter airport security and satellite surveillance of the Amazon river basin, through which the bulk of drugs passes.

Experts said the flow of drugs through the Amazon has been gaining pace as Colombia cracked down on its cartels and as U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency operations in countries like Venezuela choked off other transit routes for smugglers.

The government source said Washington should take this increase into consideration, especially as U.S. anti-drugs policies in other Latin American countries were partly to blame for the increase in cartel activity in Brazil.
Negotiations would continue, he added, saying Brasilia would wait for Washington to take the next step.
